name: Amon (Amon, the governor of Samaria under King Ahab)
title: Governor of Samaria under King Ahab
summary: Amon served as the city's chief in Samaria – a high-ranking administrative position equivalent to a governor – at the time when King Ahab ruled the northern kingdom of Israel. He appears in the biblical narrative when Ahab decides to imprison the prophet Micaiah, son of Imlah, who had foretold the king's defeat in battle at Ramoth Gilead. The king ordered that Micaiah be handed over to Amon and to Zedekiah, an official with the title "king's son," and kept imprisoned on a diet of bread and water. Amon's involvement in this event illustrates how the political and administrative machinery was used to suppress prophetic truth. Despite the attempt to silence the prophet, Micaiah's words of judgment came true when Ahab fell in battle – a reminder that God's word cannot be bound by human power.

keyEvents.title: Micaiah is handed over to Amon and Zedekiah
keyEvents.description: After the prophet Micaiah son of Imlah announced that Ahab would fall at Ramoth in Gilead, the king ordered that Micaiah be brought back to Amon, the governor, and Zedekiah, 'the king's son.' They were instructed to keep the prophet imprisoned on reduced rations of bread and water until the king returned safely.

keyEvents.title: Parallel account in Chronicles
keyEvents.description: The same event concerning Micaiah being handed over to Amon and Zedekiah is recorded in 2 Chronicles, within the context of the joint campaign by Ahab and Jehoshaphat of Judah against Ramoth in Gilead.

keyEvents.title: Ahab's fall confirms the prophecy
keyEvents.description: Ahab fell in battle at Ramoth in Gilead, just as Micaiah had predicted. This shows that the attempt to silence the prophet through imprisonment by Amon and Zedekiah could not prevent the fulfillment of God's word.

versions.summary: Amon was the governor of Samaria during King Ahab's reign in the northern kingdom of Israel. He is mentioned in connection with the prophet Micaiah's imprisonment, when King Ahab ordered that Micaiah son of Imlah be brought back to Amon, the governor of the city, and Zedekiah, the king's son, to be held prisoner until the king returned safely. Amon thus played a role in suppressing the true prophetic voice in Israel.
versions.title: Governor of Samaria
versions.reason: [major] King Ahab reigned c. 874–853 BC, that is, in the 800s BC. But the phrasing 'c. 800s BC' is somewhat imprecise and can be misunderstood as if Amon lived at the beginning of the 800s. More precisely it should read 'c. 870–850s BC' or similar to link him to Ahab's reign.; [minor] The role 'leader' is very general. It should be supplemented with a more specific role such as 'governor' or 'chief of the city' to reflect his concrete function.; [minor] The summary is good, but the phrasing 'Micaiah son of Imlah' should be consistent. In Norwegian Bible translations, 'Micaiah, son of Imlah' or 'Micaiah' is often used. It should also be clarified that Joash is described as 'the king's son,' which may refer to an official title rather than a biological son of Ahab.; [minor] The first key event (Micaiah son of Imlah prophesies against Ahab) covers a very broad verse range (vv. 8–28) and deals largely with Micaiah's prophecy in general, not specifically about Amon. For an Amon profile, the focus should be on the verses where Amon is explicitly mentioned (vv. 26–27).; [major] Footnotes are completely missing. Notes should be added concerning the Hebrew title 'sar ha-ir' (chief of the city/governor), about the administrative role this entailed, and about the parallel between 1 Kings and 2 Chronicles.

versions.summary: Amon was the city governor (Hebrew: sar ha-ir, a kind of governor) in Samaria during King Ahab's reign in the northern kingdom of Israel. He is mentioned in connection with the imprisonment of the prophet Micaiah son of Imlah. When Micaiah prophesied defeat and death for King Ahab regarding the campaign against Ramoth-gilead, the king ordered that Micaiah be taken back to Amon, the city governor, and to Zedekiah, who held the title "king's son." They were to keep the prophet imprisoned on reduced rations until the king returned in peace. Thus Amon played a role in suppressing the true prophetic voice in Israel. Ahab fell in battle, and Micaiah's prophecy was fulfilled.
versions.title: Governor of Samaria under King Ahab
versions.reason: [minor] The title is accurate and descriptive. No change needed.; [minor] Lifespan is given as 'c. 870–850s BC.' Ahab's reign was c. 874–853 BC, so this is reasonable as an active period, but the wording is slightly imprecise. "850s" could give the impression that he was active after Ahab's death. A slightly more precise formulation would be better.; [minor] The summary is good and informative, but it closely resembles the previous version (version 1) in structure and content. It should be rephrased more distinctly to avoid repetition.; [minor] The third key event (Ahab's downfall) provides relevant context, but Amon was not directly involved in this event. The description should clarify the connection with Amon even more clearly.

footnotes.text: The title 'governor' (Hebrew: שַׂר הָעִיר, sar ha-ir) refers to a high-ranking administrative official responsible for governing a city. This title appears several times in the Old Testament (see Judges 9:30; 2 Kings 23:8) and corresponds roughly to a governor or mayor. In the ancient Near East, similar positions existed in both Assyrian and Babylonian city-states.

The title 'king's son' (Hebrew: בֶּן הַמֶּלֶךְ, ben ha-melekh) used for Zedekiah was likely an official title for a royal official responsible for prison conditions or security, rather than necessarily being a biological son of the king. Similar titles are known from Mesopotamian and Egyptian administrative systems, and a seal from Judah's final kingship with the inscription 'ben ha-melekh' has been found archaeologically.

Samaria was founded as the capital by King Omri around 880 BC. Archaeological excavations at the site (Tell es-Sebastiyye) have revealed a well-developed palace area with ivory-inlaid furniture, administrative ostraca, and fortifications, testifying to a well-organized city-state with officials in various functions.

The parallel account in 2 Chronicles 18:25–26 recounts the same event as 1 Kings 22:26–27. The Chronicler has preserved this tradition but focuses more broadly on King Jehoshaphat of Judah and his alliance with Ahab. The details about Amon's role are identical in both accounts.

The expression 'bread of distress and water of distress' (Hebrew: לֶחֶם לַחַץ וּמַיִם לַחַץ) refers to a reduced ration as punishment. The same expression is used in Isaiah 30:20, but there in a figurative sense about suffering that precedes God's guidance.

The name Amon (Hebrew: אָמוֹן) is identical with the name of the Judean king Amon (2 Kings 21:18–26) and the Egyptian god Amun. It is debated whether the name shares a common Semitic root related to 'faithfulness' or 'craftsman,' or if in some cases it reflects Egyptian influence.
